
# Methods

## Overview

The carbon sequestration accounts value the CO2 that ecosystems take out of the atmosphere at a global social cost of carbon,
which is the damage that one more tonne of CO2 causes anywhere in the world. That price fits a service that benefits society as a
whole. A second question is how much of that benefit stays in the country where the sequestration happens. The country-level social
cost of carbon of @ricke2018 answers it, since it is the damage that one more tonne of CO2 causes in one country alone. This
valuation applies it to the same physical flows as the carbon sequestration accounts.

The valuation changes only the price. The actual flow and the missed flow of each country and year are those of the carbon
sequestration accounts of the same version of the tool, described in their own documentation and report, and the steps that lead
to them are not repeated here. The valuation is national, because the country-level social cost of carbon is one value for each
country, so it has no regional tables and no maps. It is kept apart from the carbon sequestration accounts, which keep their global
price, and it answers a different question. A country-level price also serves accounts of countries outside the European Union,
where the same database holds a value for most countries of the world.

## The country-level social cost of carbon

@ricke2018 estimate the social cost of carbon of each country as the present value of the change in its output that a pulse of CO2
emitted in 2020 causes up to 2200. They project output with the shared socio-economic pathways and warming with 26 climate models
and 15 carbon cycle models, and they translate the warming of each country into a change of its growth rate with the empirical
damage functions of @burke2015, which relate economic growth to temperature. The global social cost of carbon is the sum of the
values of all countries.

The database of the authors [@ricke2019db] holds the values of several damage functions, scenarios and discount rates. A decision
was made to use their reference case, which is the case that the article presents. It combines the short-run damage function of
@burke2015, the pathway SSP2 with the forcing RCP 6.0, and growth-adjusted discounting with a pure rate of time preference of
2 percent and an elasticity of the marginal utility of consumption of 1.5. The database gives the median and the 16.7 and 83.3
percent quantiles of each value, which together cover two thirds of the estimates of the uncertainty analysis. The valuation uses
the median for its central values and the two quantiles for its low and high values[\ (see the stage
[`fetch`](#code-fetch) in the code annex)]{.content-visible unless-meta="results"}.

The values can be negative. A country whose climate is cooler than the temperature at which output peaks in the damage function
gains output from moderate warming, so one more tonne of CO2 raises its output, and @ricke2018 find this for many rich northern
countries in 2020. Sequestration in those countries then has a negative value in this valuation. The authors add that trade,
migration and other links between countries can bring costs to a country whose own value is negative, and that most values turn
positive as warming continues [@ricke2018]. Malta is not in the database, so it has no value.

@tol2019 also estimates a social cost of carbon for most countries, with impact functions imputed from global estimates. That work
treats the European Union as one unit, since climate policy is set at that level, so it gives no value for the Member States and
cannot value their flows.

## From US dollars to euros

The database expresses the values in US dollars of 2005 per tonne of CO2. The valuation moves them to the euros of 2023 in the same
way as the carbon sequestration accounts move their global price, with the consumer price index of the United States from 2005 to
2023 [@bls2023cpi], a factor of 304.70/195.30, and the exchange rate of 2023, 1.0813 US dollars per euro [@ecb2023usd].[\ The
resulting factor is {{< fact cscc_factor >}} euros of 2023 per US dollar of 2005.]{.content-visible when-meta="results"} The
database does not state whether its dollars are at market exchange rates or at purchasing power parity. Open question. The
conversion treats them as US dollars.

The price $P_{c}$ of country $c$ in 2023 euros is then a real value that stays the same in every year. As in the carbon
sequestration accounts, the harmonised index of consumer prices $H$ of the European Union [@eurostat2026hicp] moves it to the euros
of each year $t$, and the deflator to the prices of 2010.

$$
P_{c,t} = P_{c}\, \frac{H_t}{H_{2023}}, \qquad V^{\text{current}}_{c,t} = F_{c,t}\, P_{c,t}, \qquad
V^{\text{constant}}_{c,t} = V^{\text{current}}_{c,t}\, \frac{H_{2010}}{H_t}
$$ {#eq-value}

Here $F_{c,t}$ is the actual flow of the country in tonnes of CO2. The missed flow is valued in the same way. The total of the
European Union adds up the values of its countries, each at its own price, and leaves out Malta[\ (see the stage
[`accounts`](#code-accounts) in the code annex)]{.content-visible unless-meta="results"}.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="results"}
@tbl-prices lists the price of each country. {{< fact cscc_negative >}} of the {{< fact cscc_countries >}} countries with a value
have a negative median, and {{< fact cscc_positive >}} a positive one. The lowest median is that of {{< fact cscc_min_country >}},
EUR {{< fact cscc_min_eur >}} per tonne of CO2, and the highest that of {{< fact cscc_max_country >}}, EUR
{{< fact cscc_max_eur >}}. The medians of the {{< fact cscc_countries >}} countries add up to EUR {{< fact cscc_eu_sum_eur >}},
against a global median of US\$ {{< fact cscc_world_usd >}} of 2005 (US\$ {{< fact cscc_world_low_usd >}} to
{{< fact cscc_world_high_usd >}}), which is EUR {{< fact cscc_world_eur >}} of 2023.

::: {#tbl-prices}
{{< datatable cscc_prices >}}

Country-level social cost of carbon per tonne of CO2 emitted in 2020, median in US dollars of 2005 as published, and low, median
and high values in euros of 2023 (Ricke et al., 2018, reference case).
:::

## Products

**Workbook.** The workbook holds a sheet of prices, with the low, median and high value of each country in US dollars of 2005 and in
euros of 2023, and sheets of the value of the actual flow and of the missed flow by country, in million euro at constant prices
of 2010 and at current prices. Each sheet gives the low, central and high value of every reporting year, and its total row adds up
the countries with a value. The physical flows are in the workbook of the carbon sequestration accounts.

## Checks

The run stops if the national flows do not cover the 27 Member States, if the database has no global value, if a median lies outside
its two quantiles, or if a value differs from the flow times its price and deflator.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="results"}
::: {#tbl-checks}
{{< datatable checks >}}

Consistency checks, with the largest gap and the tolerance that would stop the run. Gaps are relative unless they are marked as
absolute.
:::
:::
